name: Umbelliferone
lead: Umbelliferone (7-hydroxycoumarin, C9H6O3) is a natural coumarin found in plants of the carrot family (Apiaceae) such as carrot, coriander and garden angelica, and in hydrangea and asafoetida.[1] It absorbs UV light strongly at about 300 to 325 nm and fluoresces blue, and is listed on Wikipedia as having been used as a sunscreen agent as well as an optical brightener and a fluorescent indicator.[1]

Most published work concerns its use as a fluorescent probe, its metabolism, and animal and laboratory research on antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects.[2][3][4] No human trials of umbelliferone as a sunscreen or appearance product were found.

paras: Umbelliferone is a yellowish-white, odourless crystalline solid, slightly soluble in hot water and highly soluble in ethanol, and is biosynthesised from phenylalanine through cinnamic and coumaric acids.[1] It is the parent of many natural derivatives, including herniarin and the furanocoumarins such as psoralen.[1] Its glucuronides were described in 1955 and used for fluorimetric determination of beta-glucuronidase.[5]

In animal and cell models, umbelliferone has been reported to protect against cyclophosphamide-induced liver toxicity in association with Nrf2 and PPAR-gamma up-regulation,[6] and coumarins in general have been reviewed as modulators of the Keap1/Nrf2 pathway.[4][7] Grokipedia and Wikipedia also note reports of antioxidant activity and inhibition of the enzyme 17-beta-HSD type 3 in vitro.[1] Coumarin extracts from Angelica roots showed analgesic and anti-inflammatory activity in rodents.[3] Coumarins have also been reported to reduce E. coli O157:H7 biofilm formation in the laboratory.[8]

Wikipedia lists sunscreen use based on its UV absorption.[1] Its absorption in the UVB and short UVA range and its fluorescence are the properties cited; the sources reviewed contain no efficacy or safety trials of umbelliferone in commercial sunscreens, and Wikipedia flags that some claims on its page are poorly referenced.[1]
No studies found of umbelliferone as a topical photoprotective or appearance product. Related work is on coumarins generally and is laboratory or animal research.[7][9]

timeline.event: Glucuronides of umbelliferone described and used in fluorimetric enzyme assays.[5]

card.summary: Plant coumarin that absorbs UVB/short UVA and is listed as a sunscreen agent; actual evidence is lab chemistry and animal work.
card.note: No human studies as a sunscreen; Wikipedia flags weak sourcing on some uses.

quick.overview:
Umbelliferone is a natural coumarin found in carrots, coriander, angelica and hydrangea. It absorbs ultraviolet light and glows blue, which is why it appears as a sunscreen agent and a fluorescent dye.

Research on it is mostly laboratory and animal work on antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects.
quick.mechanism: The coumarin ring absorbs UV around 300 to 325 nm. In cell and animal studies it is reported to act on the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway.
quick.risks: No human safety or efficacy trials as a sunscreen were found. Its absorption shifts in alkaline conditions, and related furanocoumarins such as psoralen are distinct compounds.
